lesson.title: Unmasking Hidden Alleles: The Test Cross
lesson.summary: A test cross reveals whether an organism showing a dominant trait is homozygous or secretly heterozygous by crossing it with a homozygous recessive partner and reading the offspring.
lesson.body:
Phenotype alone cannot always tell you genotype. A pea plant with purple flowers might be PP, or it might be Pp, since the dominant allele hides the recessive one in a heterozygote. Looking at the plant gives no way to distinguish the two possibilities. The test cross is the classic solution: cross the unknown individual with a homozygous recessive partner, pp, and let the offspring reveal what gametes the unknown parent was actually producing.

A homozygous recessive tester can only ever contribute a recessive allele to its offspring, so every offspring's phenotype is determined entirely by whichever allele it received from the unknown parent. That turns the offspring into a direct readout of the unknown parent's gametes, which is exactly what a Punnett square can predict.

If the unknown parent is actually homozygous dominant, PP, the cross PP by pp produces only P gametes from one side and only p gametes from the other, so every offspring is Pp and every offspring shows the dominant purple phenotype. No white offspring appear at all, no matter how many offspring are counted.

If instead the unknown parent is heterozygous, Pp, the cross Pp by pp produces P and p gametes in equal proportion from the unknown parent, paired against only p gametes from the tester. The offspring come out as roughly half Pp, purple, and half pp, white, a one to one ratio. So the rule is simple: if any recessive offspring show up, the unknown parent must have carried a recessive allele and so was heterozygous. If a reasonably large batch of offspring are produced and every single one shows the dominant trait, the unknown parent is very likely homozygous dominant. Breeders and Mendel himself relied on exactly this technique to determine genotypes that could not be read from appearance alone.
